aaron-tufts.html.html:
Aaron Tufts of Medford enlisted for three years in the Continental Army in 1777. He served in Capt. James Bancroft’s company of Col. Michael Jackson’s regiment from March 1777 to February 1780, and went out again with Medford’s six-months men in 1780. The family record gives his birth as 18 December 1761, a son of William Tufts Jr. and Susanna (Dix) Tufts, and says that he never married.

The family record and Wild’s 1903 history of Medford say he was later of the crew of the Salem privateer Essex, captured in 1781, and that he died that year a prisoner of war in Old Mill Prison at Plymouth, England.

adam-tufts.html.html: Adam Tufts enlisted from Chelsea in February 1777 for three years in Capt. Moses Greenleaf’s company, Col. Ebenezer Francis’s regiment, which marched to Bennington and the northern army. He was reported dead on April 16, 1778. His family line is not established on this page, and his dates are not confirmed.

andrew-tufts-43-3.html.html: Andrew Tufts was born in Medford on January 6, 1761, and served as a private with the Northern Army at Saratoga. He was head of a household in 1790 and 1800, and he died at Worcester on April 20, 1836.

anne-adams-tufts.html.html:
Anne (or Anna) Adams was born in Menotomy, the northwest precinct of Cambridge that is now Arlington, a daughter of Lieut. Joseph Adams and Rachel (Allen) Adams. On April 19, 1750, she married Peter Tufts of Winter Hill, and they raised a large family on his farm there.

After the Battle of Bunker Hill she nursed the wounded, and in 1777–78 she nursed a dying woman of the Convention Army camp on Winter Hill, as told by Booth and by the Massachusetts DAR history of 1905.

barnabas-tufts.html.html: Barnabas Tufts of Gloucester served as a drummer in Col. Wigglesworth’s regiment. He was paid a travel allowance for the 360-mile journey home from Albany. The family record gives his dates as 1742/3–1795, and places him at Medford, at Gloucester on Cape Ann, and later at Topsham, Maine.

benjamin-tufts.html.html: Benjamin Tufts of Medford helped pay for the town’s soldiers sent to Canada and to New York in 1776, and served himself in Capt. Benjamin Blaney’s company of guards at Cambridge in 1778. His dates and parentage are not confirmed on this page, and whether he is the brickmaker of the Fountain Yards is not settled here.

caleb-tufts.html.html: A Caleb Tufts credited to Medford enlisted in December 1776 to guard stores at and about Boston, and served again in a company of guards in 1779. Wild’s Medford list includes a Caleb Tufts born in 1762 who later settled in Mystic, Connecticut; whether that man is the one in the Massachusetts rolls is not settled on this page.

cato-tufts.html.html: Cato Tufts of Medford was one of the men of color who served in the first years of the war. He was in Capt. Ephraim Corey’s company, Col. William Prescott’s regiment, in the camp at Cambridge in October 1775, and in 1776 he was a matross in Col. Thomas Crafts’s artillery regiment at Boston. The record ends with the note that he was “drummed out” between August and November 1776.

cotton-tufts.html.html:
Cotton Tufts was born in Medford in 1732, the son of Dr. Simon Tufts and Abigail (Smith) Tufts. He took his A.B. at Harvard College in 1749, read medicine with his older brother Dr. Simon Tufts, and by about 1751 had settled in Weymouth, where he practiced for the rest of his life. That year he became known for a treatment of diphtheria, then called the “putrid sore throat.”

He was an original member of the Massachusetts Medical Society, serving as vice-president and then president, and one of the sixty-two incorporators of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1780. No military service entry appears for him among the Tufts names in Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors.

daniel-tufts.html.html: Daniel Tufts marched with Capt. Isaac Hall’s Medford company on the Lexington alarm of April 19, 1775. In July 1778 he served with the guards stationed at Winter Hill. His dates and parents are not confirmed on this page.

david-tufts-41-7.html.html:
David Tufts was born in Medford on June 17, 1763, and the family record places him at Concord on the first day of the war; those dates would have made him about eleven, and the entry is given here as it stands. He later guarded the Convention troops, joined the Continental Army at Claverack, New York, in 1779, and enlisted again at Billerica in 1781, rising from private to corporal.

After the war he was a trader, Lynn’s first express driver, and a hotel keeper. He died at Lynn on July 6, 1823.

ebenezer-tufts-36-7.html.html: Ebenezer Tufts, a Medford brickburner, was born on March 18, 1737. He answered the Lexington alarm and later stood guard over the Convention Troops, Burgoyne’s captured army. He died on February 26, 1809.

ebenezer-tufts-87-4.html.html: Ebenezer Tufts, a farmer, was born in Medford on April 19, 1761, a son of William and Katherine (Tufts) Tufts and an older brother of Eliakim Tufts. He married Hannah Livingston at Billerica in 1781, and the family later moved to Cheshire County, New Hampshire. Hannah died at Marlborough in 1802, and he died at Roxbury, New Hampshire, on November 27, 1830. The DAR lists him as a private from Massachusetts; the rolls and pension file have not yet been checked on this page.

eliakim-tufts-87-6.html.html:
Eliakim Tufts was born in Medford on September 4, 1767, a son of William and Katherine (Tufts) Tufts. He married Sarah Ross at Billerica on May 8, 1788; their children were born at Groton, and the family later lived at Littleton, where several of the children died within a few years. After Sarah’s death he entered intentions of marriage at Littleton in 1823, and he died on February 19, 1825.

The family record notes his name on a list of Billerica men who served three years in the Continental Army; the original roll has not been seen here.

eliphalet-tufts-25-4.html.html: Eliphalet Tufts of Lee, New Hampshire, was born in 1759 and never married. He joined the Continental Army under Gen. Horatio Gates at Saratoga in 1777, was at Soldiers Fortune near West Point in 1778, and served on and off in New Hampshire regiments until he was discharged on November 11, 1781. He was living after 1807.

francis-tufts-20-1.html.html: Francis Tufts was born in Medford on July 21, 1744. He enlisted from Lincoln County, Maine, served as a private at Tiverton, Rhode Island, and at Dorchester Heights during the evacuation of Boston, and later became a Freewill Baptist minister. In 1831, in his late eighties, he set out by wagon for Ohio, and he died at Yankeetown on October 2, 1833.

francis-tufts-41-4.html.html: Francis Tufts was born in Lancaster, Massachusetts, on May 8, 1756. At the Battle of Saratoga he recovered the Continental flag from a fallen standard-bearer and led his outfit into battle with it; Gen. Horatio Gates noticed, and he was made an ensign on the spot, and a lieutenant in 1779. After the war he ran a distillery in Boston on the lane that came to be called Tufts Street. He died in Boston on August 18, 1823.

frederick-tufts-9-7.html.html: Frederick Tufts was baptized in Boston on June 27, 1731, a son of Thomas and Emma (Phipps) Tufts. The family record gives him Revolutionary service as a sergeant, credited to Mystic (West Medford), and says that he apparently died in the service or never came home; no later record of him has been found, and no muster roll naming him has yet been seen. He did not marry.

george-tufts-40-7.html.html: George Tufts was born in Medford on January 10, 1746/7, and enlisted in the army for three years. When he went home sick in 1780, the army recorded him as a deserter. He died in Concord on August 25, 1796.

grimes-tufts-40-8.html.html: Grimes Tufts, a Medford brickmaker, was born on December 4, 1748. He turned out as a minuteman on the Lexington alarm and served as an officer in Col. John Mansfield’s regiment, listed as a second lieutenant in Capt. Asa Prince’s company. He later lived in Lynn, where he died on December 23, 1808.

henry-tufts-1716.html.html: Henry Tufts was born in Medford on September 24, 1716, a son of Thomas Tufts and Mary (Lynde) Tufts. The family record says he was briefly apprenticed in physic to his uncle, Dr. Simon Tufts, before turning to tailoring in Boston, and later lived at Newmarket and Lee, New Hampshire. In 1776, at about fifty-nine, he signed the Association Test at Lee. He died in 1780.

henry-tufts-1748.html.html: Henry Tufts Jr. was born at Newmarket, New Hampshire, on June 24, 1748, the eldest son of Henry Tufts Sr. and Mary (Wedgwood) Tufts. In 1770 he married Lydia Bickford at Durham. He signed the Association Test with his father, and the family record also describes his conviction in 1793, the commuting of his sentence to imprisonment at Castle Island in Boston Harbor, and years among the Saint Francis Indians learning doctoring from Molly Ockit. He told that life in a memoir, and he died at Limerick, Maine, on January 31, 1831.

hutchinson-tufts.html.html: Hutchinson Tufts of Medford helped pay for the men the town hired to go to Canada and to New York in 1776. His dates are not confirmed on this page, and no field service is recorded for him.

isaac-tufts-36-10.html.html: Isaac Tufts was born in Medford on October 10, 1744. He answered the Lexington alarm and served as a sergeant, including at Dorchester Heights. He died on July 22, 1823.

james-tufts-82-3.html.html: James Tufts, a potter, was born in Medford on May 24, 1755, a son of James Tufts and Tabitha (Binford) Tufts. He married Elizabeth Hay at Waltham on March 23, 1775, and they had twelve children. He died in Medford on November 10, 1810. The DAR credits him with service as a corporal and as a private; no company or regiment is given in that summary, and no muster roll naming him has yet been found here.

james-tufts-jr-36-2.html.html: James Tufts Jr., a Medford farmer, was born on January 15, 1726. He is credited with fetching gunsmith’s tools from Charlestown in March 1775, among the town’s early acts of resistance. He died on November 5, 1786.

john-tufts-19-5.html.html: John Tufts of Malden was born in Medford on March 15, 1738/9, a son of Benjamin and Mary (Hutchinson) Tufts. In June 1776 he went with Capt. Benjamin Blaney’s company on the expedition to Point Shirley, now Winthrop. He was head of a household in the 1790 census and died at Malden in 1799; the family record gives the day as March 23, and the DAR as February 23.

john-tufts-22-1.html.html: John Tufts of Windham, Connecticut, was born on October 25, 1755, and served three tours: north to Ticonderoga in 1775, at the siege of Boston and in New York in 1776, and in the Hudson Highlands in 1778. He later lived at Ashford, at Stephentown, New York, and at Ludlow, Massachusetts, where he was still living after 1835.

john-tufts-49-2.html.html: John Tufts served as a private in the Revolution and farmed on Prospect Hill, in what is now Somerville. An inventory of his estate listed $6,390 in real estate and $1,195 in personal property. His birth and death dates are not recorded in the entry on this page.

john-tufts-53-3.html.html:
John Tufts was born on November 24, 1754, in Charlestown, the second son of Peter Tufts of Winter Hill and Anne Adams Tufts, and the younger brother of Peter Tufts Jr. On the morning of April 19, 1775, his father rode out on Paul Revere’s alarm, and family accounts say John was charged to stay behind. Ellen Chase, drawing on Jones, tells that he followed on, up beyond Lexington, and that while crossing one of the hills he met Elizabeth Perry, running from her blazing home; he guarded her to her relatives, and they later married. Samuel Abbot Smith, in an 1864 address at West Cambridge, told the same meeting on the authority of their son Oliver.

Booth calls him a scientific farmer and gardener. During the Revolution his father established him on a farm whose house Booth calls the headquarters of General Lee; the place stayed in the family through Oliver, who was born and died there. John served as a minuteman at the Lexington alarm and as a corporal under Capt. Isaac Hall of Medford. In 1806 he was considered non compos; in 1817 he was dismissed from the First Church, Charlestown, to join the Second Church. He died on September 9, 1839, leaving an estate of $16,909.

jonathan-tufts-36-8.html.html: Jonathan Tufts, a brickmaker of Medford, was born on February 25, 1739, and served as a private in the lines around Boston. He died on September 26, 1784.

joseph-tufts-1755.html.html: Joseph Tufts Jr. was born on February 17, 1755, the son of Capt. Joseph Tufts and Hannah (Cutter) Tufts of Medford. At twenty-one he helped pay the bounties that sent Medford men to Canada in the summer of 1776, and the family record also calls him a private in the Revolution. He married his cousin Esther Dickson at Menotomy on December 23, 1779, was taxed in Medford until 1794, and later headed a household in Danvers, where he died on March 10, 1840.

joseph-tufts-jr-15-2.html.html: Joseph Tufts Jr. of Medford was born on February 21, 1730/1. He served the Revolution at home, on the town’s Committee of Correspondence and Safety, and died on December 6, 1778.

moses-tufts-40-6.html.html: Moses Tufts, a schoolteacher, was baptized on October 7, 1744. He served as first lieutenant in Capt. Isaac Hall’s company at Dorchester Heights and went north with the Canadian expedition of 1776. He later lived at Chelsea and at Newcastle, Maine, and died about 1805.

nathan-tuffs-35-9.html.html: Nathan Tuffs was born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on December 16, 1752. He fought from Lexington to Yorktown: an artilleryman in Knox’s regiment, a prisoner after Fort Washington, and a three-year man in the 13th Massachusetts. He died at Bethel, Vermont, on August 5, 1827.

nathan-tufts-15-7.html.html: Nathan Tufts of Medford was born on October 5, 1741. He supported the war by lending toward the bounties paid to enlisting men in 1776; no military service is recorded for him in this entry. He died on June 12, 1784.

nathan-tufts-jr.html.html: Nathan Tufts Jr. of Medford helped pay for the men sent to New York in 1776 and served 82 days with Capt. Benjamin Blaney’s guards at Cambridge in 1778. His dates are not confirmed on this page.

peter-tufts-jr.html.html: Peter Tufts Jr. was born on January 9, 1753, at Woburn, the son of Peter and Anne (Adams) Tufts of Winter Hill. On April 19, 1775, the day his parents marked their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary, he marched from Medford with Capt. Isaac Hall’s company on the Lexington alarm. Medford later listed his name on its monument to the town’s First Company of Minute Men. He also served as a Charlestown selectman, including the years 1806 to 1817. This page gives his death as November 4, 1832; Wild prints 1836.

peter-tufts-winter-hill.html.html: Peter Tufts, called “of Winter Hill,” was born on April 24, 1728, the second son of Peter Tufts of Milk Row and Lydia Bucknam, and was established on a farm on Winter Hill. On the night of April 18–19, 1775, the alarm came to his door; the day was also his twenty-fifth wedding anniversary. The family list of Revolutionary service names him a Medford minuteman of Winter Hill; no muster roll naming this Peter has been matched. He died on March 4, 1791.

samuel-tufts-11-5.html.html: Samuel Tufts was born in Medford on January 7, 1734/5, a son of Dr. Simon Tufts and Abigail (Smith) Tufts and a younger brother of Dr. Simon and Dr. Cotton Tufts. He practiced as a physician in Newbury and Newburyport, and in 1777 he served in the commissary of Capt. Newell’s company. He died on September 20, 1799.

samuel-tufts-15-3.html.html: Samuel Tufts was born in Medford on August 16, 1732. He was forty-two when Paul Revere’s alarm reached Medford, and he answered it. He later sat on the town’s Committee of Safety, and he was the father of the Revolutionary soldiers Samuel 3rd and Caleb. He died on December 31, 1818.

samuel-tufts-18-5.html.html:
Samuel Tufts, a farmer, was born at Charlestown on November 24, 1737, a son of Peter Tufts and Lydia (Bucknam) Tufts, and lived on Milk Row. On the night of April 18, 1775, he was still up, casting bullets with his slave in a hut behind the house, when the British column went quietly by. A neighbor, the widow Rand, ran across the road to tell him; when his lantern showed the footprints in the dirt road, he rode by a bridle path to Cambridge to spread the alarm.

He later served as a private, was town treasurer of Charlestown in 1777–1778 and 1780 and a selectman in 1780, and died on October 24, 1828.

samuel-tufts-3d.html.html: Samuel Tufts 3d of Medford marched with Capt. Isaac Hall’s company on April 19, 1775. Medford had at least three men of the name at the time, and the numeral set him apart from the others. His dates and parents are not confirmed on this page.

samuel-tufts-41-2.html.html: Samuel Tufts 2nd was born in Medford on August 19, 1752. He answered the Lexington alarm, served as a private in the Canada campaign of 1776 and at West Point in 1780, and was head of a household in Medford in 1790 and 1810. He died on November 29, 1815.

samuel-tufts-44-3.html.html: Samuel Tufts 3rd, son of Samuel and brother of Caleb, was born in Medford on April 16, 1761. He served as a private at West Point and in Canada. By trade he was a fagot maker, binding the bundles of branches used to fill deep trenches before drain pipes. He died on August 29, 1803.

simon-tufts-11-1.html.html:
Simon Tufts of Medford was born on January 16, 1726/7, the eldest child of Dr. Simon Tufts and Abigail (Smith) Tufts. He graduated from Harvard College in 1744, read medicine with his father, and took over the practice at his father’s death.

An ardent Whig and a justice of the peace from 1770, he took depositions and bound wounds after Lexington and Concord, and attended the wounded on both sides at Bunker Hill. He also lent bounty money for the war, and reluctantly served as conservator of a Loyalist neighbor’s estate. He died in Medford on December 31, 1786.

stephen-tufts-21-1.html.html: Stephen Tufts Jr. was born at Malden on March 28, 1749, the eldest son of Stephen Tufts, schoolmaster, and Katherine (Taylor) Tufts. He owned the mill privileges on Spot Pond Brook and lived in the old Tufts house on the bank of the Malden River. He served as a private at the Lexington alarm in 1775, in Col. Thomas Gardner’s regiment, and died on March 12, 1832.

thomas-tufts-25-3.html.html: Thomas Tufts of Lee, New Hampshire, was born in 1757. He served as a private in the Revolution and later as a town highway surveyor. He died in 1834.

timothy-tufts.html.html: On the afternoon of April 19, 1775, Lord Percy’s column, falling back from Lexington and Concord, turned off toward Charlestown and passed Timothy Tufts’s door on the road now called Elm Street. He served Charlestown’s Milk Row school as a committeeman from 1776, and later as moderator, selectman, and justice of the peace. No military service record has yet been matched to him in Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors. He was born in 1735 and died in 1805.

timothy-tufts-21-4.html.html: Timothy Tufts was born at Malden on April 15, 1756, a son of Stephen and Katherine (Taylor) Tufts. He served as a corporal in the Revolution: he answered the Lexington alarm with Capt. Benjamin Blaney, went on the Point Shirley expedition in June 1776, and on September 26, 1776, was drafted and marched as third corporal. He later became a master mariner and died at Baltimore in April 1810.

william-tuffs-35-8.html.html: William Tuffs—the family name spelled the old way—went west after the war and died in Indiana in 1848, at the age the family record gives as ninety-seven. His own pension affidavit, as reported in the family record, places his birth on September 20, 1750, at Mystic, or West Medford. A DAR chapter in Elkhart bears his name.

william-tufts-13-6.html.html: William Tufts was born in Charlestown on June 10, 1713, a generation older than most of the family’s Revolutionary soldiers. He had helped build Fort Lawrence on the Bay of Fundy. For some years the family lived in Lancaster, where the selectmen warned them out on January 6, 1767, listing the household as having come from Medford. He died at Medford on October 29, 1783.

william-tufts-1777.html.html: William Tufts was born in Medford on August 24, 1762, a son of William Tufts Jr. and Catherine (Tufts) Tufts. Wild lists his service at the lines at Boston in 1776 and in Col. Wesson’s regiment in 1777, and says he was killed in 1777. The family record says he was a private killed at the Battle of Bennington in August 1777; the day and place have not been confirmed from a muster or casualty roll on this page.

william-tufts-40-2.html.html: William Tufts Jr. of Medford was born on March 27, 1736, and served as a private in a company of guards near Boston late in the war. He died on April 27, 1782.

zachariah-tufts.html.html: Two entries under the name Zachariah Tufts of Woburn appear in Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors. The first follows a private in Capt. John Wood’s company through 1775, in camp at Medford and Cambridge. The second is a 1780 descriptive list of a man aged 21, engaged for Woburn for three years. Whether the two entries name the same man is not established on this page.
